intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 associated with acetylcholine receptor deficiency (CMS11) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding rapsyn (RAPSN; 601592) on chromosome 11p11.2.

checks.evidence_quote: we identify three recessive rapsyn mutations: one patient carries L14P in TPR1 and N88K in TPR3; two are homozygous for N88K; and one carries N88K and 553ins5
checks.explanation: Recessive rapsyn mutations, both homozygous and compound heterozygous, cause EP AChR deficiency CMS; CMS11 label is nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Congenital myasthenic syndrome-11 (CMS11) is an autosomal recessive postsynaptic disorder of the neuromuscular junction in which acetylcholine receptors (AChR) are deficient at the endplate. Rapsyn plays an essential role in clustering and anchoring AChR at the postsynaptic membrane, and the RAPSN mutations reduce coclustering of AChR with rapsyn (Ohno et al., 2002). Engel et al. (2015) noted that most patients present in the first year of life and a few present later. Burke et al. (2003) distinguished an early-onset phenotype, frequently associated with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita and life-threatening crises, from a late-onset phenotype that develops in adolescence or adulthood. Hypotonia and respiratory difficulty at birth were reported by Das et al. (2014). Most patients respond well to acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, and some derive additional benefit from 3,4-diaminopyridine (Engel et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Burke et al. (2003) described 2 distinct phenotypes among patients with rapsyn mutations, early-onset and late-onset. The early-onset phenotype was frequently associated with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita and life-threatening crises. The late-onset phenotype developed in adolescence or adulthood and was initially mistaken for seronegative myasthenia gravis.

paragraphs.text: In 4 patients with congenital myasthenic syndrome and endplate AChR deficiency, Ohno et al. (2002) identified mutations in the RAPSN gene. All of the patients carried the asn88-to-lys (N88K) mutation, either in the homozygous state or in compound heterozygosity with a second RAPSN mutation. In expression studies, the mutant rapsyn was less able to cocluster AChR.
